To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PEGylation improves the pharmacokinetic profile of a chemokine-derived mutant without compromising its biological function.
PEGylation improves the serum half-life and efficacy of a dominant-negative CXCL-8 mutant in vivo.
PEGylation improves bioavailability and serum clearance of a dominant-negative CXCL mutant and reduces neutrophil infiltration in a murine model.

The main takeaway from our work is that

PEGylation does not significantly influence the bioactivity of chemokine-based biologics, and therefore it can be used for the development of new therapeutics for the treatment of inflammatory diseases.
